name: Cryptography
description: Applied cryptography: symmetric and asymmetric encryption, hashing, digital signatures, TLS and secure password storage.

questions.question: Which of the following is a symmetric encryption algorithm?
options: RSA
ECDSA
AES
Diffie-Hellman
questions.explanation: AES uses the same secret key to encrypt and decrypt. RSA and ECDSA are asymmetric, and Diffie-Hellman is a key-exchange protocol.

questions.question: Which statement about a cryptographic hash function such as SHA-256 is true?
options: The same input always produces the same fixed-length output, and the input cannot practically be recovered from it
It can be decrypted with the right key
Its output length grows with the size of the input
Two different inputs always produce the same output
questions.explanation: Hash functions are deterministic, produce a fixed-length digest, and are one-way (preimage resistant); they are not encryption and have no key.

questions.question: Why should a unique random salt be added to each password before hashing?
options: It makes the hash reversible for password recovery
It shortens the hash so it uses less storage
It replaces the need for a slow hashing algorithm
It ensures identical passwords produce different hashes and defeats precomputed rainbow tables
questions.explanation: Salts make each hash unique, so attackers cannot use precomputed tables or spot users sharing a password. A slow algorithm is still needed.

questions.question: In a typical TLS connection, how are asymmetric and symmetric cryptography used?
options: All application data is encrypted with the server's RSA public key
Asymmetric cryptography authenticates the server and establishes shared keys; symmetric ciphers then encrypt the bulk data
Symmetric keys are sent in plaintext and then used for signatures
Only hashing is used, so no encryption keys are needed
questions.explanation: TLS uses certificates/signatures and key exchange (e.g. ECDHE) to authenticate and agree on session keys, then fast symmetric ciphers like AES-GCM for data.

questions.question: Why is ECB mode considered insecure for encrypting most data with a block cipher?
options: It requires a key longer than 512 bits
It cannot be decrypted without the initialization vector
Identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks, leaking patterns in the data
It only works with asymmetric algorithms
questions.explanation: ECB encrypts each block independently with no IV, so repeated plaintext blocks are visible as repeated ciphertext blocks. Modes like GCM avoid this.

questions.question: Which approach is the best choice for storing user passwords in a new application?
options: SHA-256 with no salt
AES-256 encryption with the key stored in the application config
MD5 with a per-user salt
Argon2id with a unique per-user salt and tuned cost parameters
questions.explanation: Passwords should be hashed with a slow, memory-hard password hashing function like Argon2id (or bcrypt/scrypt). Fast hashes are easy to brute force and encryption is reversible.

practical.title: Explain secure password storage
practical.instructions: A teammate proposes encrypting user passwords with AES so they can be decrypted later. In 3-5 sentences, explain why passwords should be hashed instead of encrypted, and describe how they should be hashed (name a suitable algorithm and the role of a salt).
practical.expected_output: Explains that hashing is one-way while encryption is reversible and depends on protecting a key; recommends a slow password-hashing algorithm such as Argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt or PBKDF2 with a unique per-user salt to defeat rainbow tables and slow brute force.

rubric.hint: Explain that a hash is one-way: the original password cannot be recovered from it.

rubric.description: Explains the risk of reversible encryption / key exposure
rubric.hint: Encryption can be reversed by anyone who obtains the key, so a key leak exposes every password.
Use a deliberately slow password hashing function such as Argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt or PBKDF2.

rubric.description: Describes the use of a salt
rubric.hint: Mention a unique random salt per password to defeat rainbow tables.

tasks.title: Learn the building blocks of cryptography
tasks.description: Work through the Khan Academy cryptography unit covering ciphers, keys and modern public-key ideas. Write short definitions of symmetric encryption, asymmetric encryption, hashing and digital signatures.
tasks.completion_criteria: Notes with a correct one-paragraph definition and example use for each of the four primitives.

tasks.title: Hash and compare files
tasks.description: Create two text files that differ by one character and compute their SHA-256 hashes with sha256sum or PowerShell Get-FileHash. Observe how a tiny change produces a completely different digest.
tasks.completion_criteria: Screenshot or notes showing both hashes and a sentence explaining the avalanche effect.

tasks.title: Implement secure password hashing
tasks.description: In a small script, hash and verify passwords using a library for Argon2id or bcrypt, following the OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet. Confirm that hashing the same password twice yields different stored values.
tasks.completion_criteria: A working script with hash and verify functions plus a test showing correct and incorrect passwords are handled properly.

tasks.title: Audit an application's cryptographic choices
tasks.description: Review one of your own projects (or an open-source app) against the OWASP Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet. Document how secrets, passwords, data at rest and data in transit are protected and propose fixes for weak choices.
tasks.completion_criteria: A written review covering at least four areas with findings and concrete remediation recommendations.
